posts.post_title: Pulsation Rate in Machine Milking
posts.post_content: In machine milking, pulsation rate (per minute) should be:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 55–65

The recommended pulsation rate in machine milking is 55–65 cycles per minute. The optimum is 60 cycles per minute. The rate should not be less than 40 or more than 120 cycles per minute.

Key Machine Milking Parameters
  • Optimum pulsation rate: 60 cycles/minute
  • Pulsation ratio for cattle: 60:40 (milk phase : rest phase)
  • Pulsation ratio for buffalo: 50:50
  • Ideal vacuum for cattle: 352 mmHg
  • Ideal vacuum for buffalo: 400 mmHg
  • Minimum herd size for machine milking: 20 animals
  • Heart of milking machine: Pulsator
Functions of Milking Machine
  1. Opens streak canal with partial vacuum → allows continuous milk flow.
  2. Massages teats → prevents blood congestion in the teat.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 35–45 → too slow; may not adequately stimulate milk ejection.
  • 65–75 → slightly above the ideal range.
  • 40–60 → partially correct but does not capture the ideal range of 55–65 with optimum at 60.

posts.post_title: TDN Requirement per Litre of Milk
posts.post_content: TDN required by cow for 1 liter of milk production is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 0.32 kg TDN

A dairy cow requires 0.32 kg of TDN (Total Digestible Nutrients) for the production of 1 liter of milk. This is the production allowance over and above the maintenance requirement.

What is TDN?

TDN is a measure of the energy value of a feed — it is the sum of digestible crude protein, digestible crude fiber, digestible nitrogen-free extract, and 2.25 × digestible ether extract. It represents the total digestible portion of a feed that provides energy.

Key Nutrient Requirements of Dairy Cows
  • Maintenance TDN: based on body weight of the cow.
  • Production allowance: 0.32 kg TDN per litre of milk.
  • Milk fat synthesis: Acetate (a VFA produced in the rumen) is the primary precursor for milk fat synthesis.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 0.45 kg → overestimate for production requirement.
  • 0.50 kg → too high; this would be excessive.
  • 0.55 kg → even higher; well above the standard production allowance.

posts.post_title: Dairy Product by Lactic Fermentation of Standardized Milk
posts.post_content: A coagulated product obtained from pasteurized or boiled standardized milk by lactic fermentation is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Yoghurt

Yoghurt is a coagulated product obtained from pasteurized or boiled standardized milk by lactic fermentation. It is a Western-origin fermented milk product, distinct from Dahi (Indian curd).

Yoghurt vs. Dahi
  • Yoghurt: Made from pasteurized/boiled standardized milk; specific starter cultures (Streptococcus thermophilus + Lactobacillus bulgaricus); coagulated product with controlled acidity.
  • Dahi: Indian curd; made with 0.5–1% starter (previous day's dahi or buttermilk); not necessarily standardized milk; traditional method.
Classification of Indian Dairy Products
  • Concentrated whole milk: Khoa, Kheer, Basundi, Kulfi
  • Coagulated milk products: Dahi, Srikhand, Paneer, Channa
  • Clarified butterfat products: Makhan, Ghee, Lassi
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Shrikhand → a semi-soft sweetish-sour product made from dahi by straining whey; secondary fermented product.
  • Channa → obtained by acid coagulation of hot milk and drainage of whey; not by lactic fermentation.
  • Lassi → desi buttermilk (by-product of butter churning); not a coagulated fermented milk.

posts.post_title: Thickening Agents Used in Milk
posts.post_content: Which of the following is/are thickening agent(s) used in milk?

_aimcq_options.text: All of the above (Cane sugar, Gelatin, Starch)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

The thickening agents used in milk are Cane sugar (sucrose), Gelatin, and Starch — all three are used to increase the consistency and body of milk products.

Detection of These Adulterants/Additives
  • Starch: Detected by Iodine solution test — gives blue colour.
  • Gelatin: Detected by Picric acid solution.
  • Cane sugar: Refractometer or chemical tests.
Other Additives in Milk
  • Preservatives: Boric acid, Borax, Benzoic acid, Formalin, H₂O₂, Salicylic acid, Na₂CO₃, NaHCO₃
  • Natural preservatives: Lactoperoxidase, Lactoferrin, Conglutinin
  • Colouring agents: Annatto, Coal tar dye, Turmeric

posts.post_title: Composition of Solid-Not-Fat (SNF) in Milk
posts.post_content: Solid-Not-Fat (SNF) of milk is composed of:

_aimcq_options.text: All of the above (Protein, Lactose, and Ash)

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

SNF (Solid-Not-Fat) refers to all components of milk solids excluding fat. It includes Protein, Lactose, and Ash (minerals).

Milk Composition Breakdown
  • Total Solids (TS) = Fat + SNF
  • Fat = Phospholipids + Cholesterol + Carotene + Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)
  • SNF = Lactose (milk sugar) + Proteins (Casein + Whey) + Ash (minerals) + Others
SNF Standards (PFA-1976)
  • Buffalo/Sheep/Goat/Double toned milk: 9.0% SNF
  • Skim milk: 8.7% SNF
  • Cow/Toned/Standard/Recombined milk: 8.5% SNF

posts.post_title: Milk Component Responsible for Texture and Miscibility of Milk Products
posts.post_content: The milk component responsible for the texture and miscibility of milk products is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lactose

Lactose is responsible for the texture and miscibility of milk products. It acts as a structural component in many dairy products, affecting their texture, body, and how they mix with other ingredients.

Role of Lactose in Milk
  • Present as a True Solution in milk
  • Least variable component of milk (most constant)
  • Average lactose content: Cow milk — 4.5%, Buffalo milk — 4.8%
  • Responsible for the typical sweetness of milk
  • Acts as energy source for lactic acid bacteria (starter cultures)
Commercial Importance of Milk Components
  • Most commercially important: Fat
  • Most constant: Lactose (and freezing point)
  • Most variable: Fat

posts.post_title: Classification of Mammary Glands
posts.post_content: Mammary glands are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Modified sudoriferous (sweat) glands

Mammary glands are modified sudoriferous (sweat) glands — ectodermal in origin. This is an important embryological classification.

Key Anatomical Facts about Mammary Glands (Udder)
  • Ectodermal in origin (derived from the ectoderm layer of the embryo).
  • Innervated only by sympathetic fibres; parasympathetic fibres are absent in the udder.
  • No communication exists among all 4 quarters of the udder — this minimizes the spread of infection within the udder.
Suspensory Structures of the Udder
  • Median suspensory ligament (elastic) — primarily responsible for udder breakdown.
  • Two lateral suspensory ligaments (non-elastic).
  • Skin.
Blood Supply
  • Arterial: External pudic artery (mammary artery)
  • 400–500 ml of blood must pass through udder to produce 1 ml of milk.
  • Subcutaneous abdominal vein (milk vein) acts as index for milking ability.

posts.post_title: Storage Sites of Milk in Animals
posts.post_content: Storage site(s) of milk in animals include:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Alveoli, Glands and Cisterns

Milk is stored in all three compartments: alveoli, glands (ducts), and cisterns within the mammary gland. However, the proportion varies significantly between species.

Proportion of Milk in Cistern vs. Alveoli (Cistern:Alveolus ratio)
  • Goat: 80:20 → 80% in cistern (can be milked anytime — no oxytocin reflex needed)
  • Sheep: 50:50
  • Cattle: 30:70
  • Buffalo and Camel: 5:95 (mostly in alveoli)
  • Sow: 0:100 (all in alveoli)
Clinical Significance
  • Goats store 80% milk in cisterns — this is why milk can be drawn at any time from goats without oxytocin reflex/let-down stimulus.
  • Sows store all milk in alveoli — piglets must constantly stimulate the udder for milk let-down.
  • Residual milk (left after normal milking) is mainly in alveoli — requires oxytocin injection or re-milking to obtain.

posts.post_title: Standard Milk Composition
posts.post_content: Standard milk contains:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 4.5% Fat & 8.5% SNF

According to the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA-1976), Standard milk must contain a minimum of 4.5% Fat and 8.5% SNF (Solid-Not-Fat).

Milk Fat Standards (PFA-1976)
  • Skim milk: 0.5% fat
  • Double toned milk: 1.5% fat
  • Toned milk / Sheep / Goat / Recombined: 3.0% fat
  • Cow milk: 3.5% fat
  • Standard milk: 4.5% fat
  • Buffalo milk: 5.0% fat
SNF Standards (PFA-1976)
  • Buffalo / Sheep / Goat / Double toned milk: 9.0% SNF
  • Skim milk: 8.7% SNF
  • Cow / Toned / Standard / Recombined milk: 8.5% SNF

Standard milk is essentially a mix blended to meet these legal minimums, serving as the baseline market milk grade in India.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 5% Fat & 8.5% SNF — that's the standard for Buffalo milk fat, not standard milk.
  • 3% Fat & 9% SNF — matches Toned milk fat with Buffalo/Sheep SNF; incorrect combination.
  • 5% Fat & 8.7% SNF — no recognized milk category matches this combination.

posts.post_title: Buffalo: Lactation with Maximum Milk Yield
posts.post_content: In Buffalo, maximum milk yield takes place in which lactation?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 4th lactation

In Buffalo, the maximum milk yield occurs during the 4th lactation. After this, yield gradually declines with successive lactations.

Comparison: Cow vs. Buffalo
  • Cow: Maximum milk yield occurs in the 4th–6th lactation.
  • Buffalo: Maximum milk yield in 4th lactation.
Lactation Curve Pattern

Both cow and buffalo follow a typical lactation curve — milk yield rises steeply post-calving, peaks at 6–8 weeks, then gradually declines. With successive parities (lactations), the peak yield increases until the optimum lactation, after which it declines due to ageing effects on mammary tissue.

Economic Implication

Culling decisions in dairy animals are often made after the optimum lactation number, since yields decline thereafter and maintenance costs remain high.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 3rd → not the peak lactation for buffalo; yield is still increasing.
  • 6th → peak for cow (range 4th–6th), not buffalo.
  • 8th → too late; by this lactation, both cow and buffalo are well past peak production.

posts.post_title: Correct Method of Milking Dairy Animals
posts.post_content: The correct method of milking dairy animals is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fisting (Full Hand Method)

Fisting (Full Hand Method) is the correct and best method of milking dairy animals. The teat is grasped with all five fingers and pressed against the palm, squeezing milk downward in a rhythmic motion that mimics the suckling action of a calf.

Three Methods of Hand Milking
  • Fisting / Full hand method: All 5 fingers grasp the teat and press against the palm. Best method — natural, mimics calf suckling, no teat injury.
  • Knuckling: Thumb bent/knuckled against teat. Wrong method — causes teat injury, may lead to mastitis.
  • Stripping: Teat held between thumb and forefinger and drawn downward. Used mainly for: (a) removing left milk after machine milking, (b) sheep and goat with small teats, (c) towards completion of milking.
Other Milking Guidelines
  • Always milk from the left side of the cow.
  • Foremilk should not be mixed with the rest (contains high bacterial count).
  • Ideal inter-milking interval: 12 hours.
  • After machine milking, remaining milk is removed by stripping.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Knuckling → causes teat injury; a wrong and harmful method.
  • Stripping → a supplementary method, not the primary/correct milking method.

posts.post_title: Frozen Dairy Product from Pasteurized Milk
posts.post_content: A frozen dairy product made by the rapid freezing of pasteurized milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ice cream

Ice cream is a frozen dairy product made by the rapid freezing of pasteurized milk (or cream) along with sugar, flavouring agents, stabilizers, and emulsifiers. It is a Western-origin product.

Ice Cream vs. Kulfi
  • Ice cream: Frozen dairy product from pasteurized milk; Western origin; uses a freezer with agitation (to incorporate air/overrun); ingredients include cream, sugar, stabilizer (gelatin), flavour.
  • Kulfi: Indigenous Indian frozen dairy product; made from concentrated (khoa-based) milk; frozen without agitation; denser texture; no overrun; traditionally frozen in sealed conical moulds.
Stabilizer/Thickening Agents in Milk Products
  • Thickening agents: Cane sugar (sucrose), Starch, Gelatin
  • Flavouring agent in butter: Diacetyl (≤4 ppm)
  • Yellow colour of butter: Annatto
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Cream → a dairy product with high fat content obtained by separation, not a frozen product.
  • Srikhand → a semi-soft fermented product; not frozen.
  • Channa → acid-coagulated fresh milk product; not frozen.

posts.post_title: Colour of Milk from Stall-fed Cow
posts.post_content: Stall-fed cow yields milk of which colour?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: White-yellowish milk

Stall-fed cows (fed on dry fodder, concentrates, and stored feed with limited green pasture) yield white-yellowish milk due to moderate β-carotene content from stored feed.

Colour of Milk — Key Comparisons
  • Stall-fed cow: White-yellowish milk (moderate carotene)
  • Grass-fed cattle: Yellow-coloured milk (high β-carotene from fresh green grass)
  • Buffalo milk: Pure white — buffalo converts all β-carotene to Vitamin A, so no carotene remains to colour the milk.
  • Cow milk: Yellowish — cannot fully convert β-carotene; excess carotene gives yellow tint.
Responsible Pigment

The colour of milk fat depends on its β-carotene content — not riboflavin or thiamine.

posts.post_title: Protective Factor in Colostrum That Protects Immunoglobulins
posts.post_content: Colostrum of ruminants contains ___________ which protects immunoglobulins from digestion in GIT of calf:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Trypsin inhibitor

Ruminant colostrum contains a Trypsin inhibitor that protects immunoglobulins (antibodies) from being digested by proteolytic enzymes in the gastrointestinal tract of the newborn calf.

Why This Is Important
  • In ruminants, placental transfer of antibodies does NOT occur (unlike humans).
  • The newborn calf is entirely dependent on colostrum for passive immunity.
  • The gut of the calf can absorb intact immunoglobulins only in the first 24–36 hours of life (intestinal closure).
  • Trypsin inhibitor ensures the IgG molecules reach the intestine intact for absorption.
Other Colostrum Key Facts
  • Predominant immunoglobulin in bovine colostrum: IgG
  • Major immunoglobulin in human colostrum: IgA
  • Colostrum fed @ 10% of body weight (or 2–2.5 L/day for 3–4 days)
  • Milk loses colostral properties within 72 hours (3–4 days) after parturition

posts.post_title: Vitamins in Milk — True Statements
posts.post_content: Which of the following is/are true about vitamins present in milk?

_aimcq_options.text: All of the above: Milk is a poor source of Vitamin C; Cow milk is rich in Vitamin A & Carotene; Milk is a good source of thiamine & riboflavin
Only: Milk is a poor source of Vitamin C
Only: Cow milk is particularly rich in Vitamin A and Carotene
Only: Milk is a good source of thiamine and riboflavin

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All of the above

All three statements about vitamins in milk are correct.

Vitamins in Milk — Key Facts
  • Milk is a POOR source of Vitamin C ✔ — Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is present in very small amounts and is further lost during pasteurization and sterilization.
  • Cow milk is rich in Vitamin A and Carotene ✔ — Cow milk contains β-carotene (precursor of Vitamin A), unlike buffalo milk which converts it all to Vitamin A.
  • Milk is a GOOD source of Thiamine (B1) and Riboflavin (B2) ✔ — particularly riboflavin, which gives whey its greenish-yellow colour.
Vitamins Lost During Processing
  • Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) and Vitamin C — lost during pasteurization and sterilization
  • Irradiated milk — Vitamin D content increased by UV ray treatment

posts.post_title: Ligament Responsible for Udder Breakdown
posts.post_content: Which ligament is elastic and primarily responsible for udder breakdown?

_aimcq_options.text: Both median and lateral suspensory ligaments

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Median suspensory ligament

The median suspensory ligament is elastic and is primarily responsible for udder breakdown. When it weakens (due to genetics, age, or repeated pregnancies), the udder drops — this is termed udder breakdown.

Suspensory Structures of the Udder
  • Median suspensory ligament: Elastic → responsible for udder breakdown when weakened.
  • Two lateral suspensory ligaments: Non-elastic (fibrous) → provide firm lateral support.
  • Skin: Provides external support.
Why This Distinction Matters
  • Cows with weak median suspensory ligaments have pendulous (low-hanging) udders, which are more prone to injury, mastitis, and difficulty in machine milking.
  • Udder attachment scores are used in dairy cattle breeding programmes to select against udder breakdown.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Lateral suspensory ligament → non-elastic; it provides support but is NOT responsible for udder breakdown.
  • Both → only the median ligament is elastic; the laterals are not.
  • Inguinal ligament → not a suspensory structure of the udder.

posts.post_title: Nature of K-Casein (Kappa-Casein) in Milk
posts.post_content: K-casein (κ-casein) present in milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Calcium-insensitive casein

K-casein (κ-casein) is calcium-insensitive casein — it is NOT precipitated by calcium ions. This is a defining feature that distinguishes it from the other major casein fractions.

Types of Casein Proteins in Milk
  • Three types: α-casein, β-casein, γ-casein
  • α-casein consists of two components:
    • αs-casein (alpha-s casein): Calcium-sensitive — precipitated by calcium ions.
    • κ-casein (K-casein): Calcium-insensitive — NOT precipitated by calcium ions.
Role of K-Casein
  • K-casein acts as a protective colloid — it stabilizes the casein micelle in milk by preventing calcium-mediated aggregation.
  • When K-casein is hydrolyzed by chymosin (rennet), the micelle destabilizes and coagulation (curd formation) occurs — this is the basis of cheese making.
Casein in Milk — Summary
  • Casein exists in milk as calcium-caseinate-phosphate complex (colloidal suspension).
  • Casein = 80% of total milk protein; responsible for white colour and viscosity of milk.
  • Cow milk casein: 3%; Buffalo milk casein: 4.3%.

posts.post_title: HTST Pasteurization Protocol
posts.post_content: Temperature-time protocol for HTST pasteurization is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 72°C / 15 seconds

HTST (High Temperature Short Time) pasteurization, also called Flash pasteurization, uses 72°C for 15 seconds. It is the modern commercial method of pasteurization.

All Pasteurization Methods at a Glance
  • LTLT (Low Temperature Long Time / Batch / Holding): 63°C / 30 minutes
  • HTST (Flash pasteurization): 72°C / 15 seconds ✔
  • Stassanization: 74°C / 7 seconds
  • UHT (Ultra High Temperature): 130–135°C / fraction of a second
  • Uperization (Ultra-pasteurization): 150°C / fraction of a second
  • Vacuum pasteurization (Vacreation): by Vacreator using direct steam under reduced pressure
Key Points on HTST
  • HTST is the most widely used method at commercial/industrial level.
  • Index organism for pasteurization is Coxiella burnetti (causative agent of Q-fever) — it is the most heat-resistant pathogen destroyed by pasteurization.
  • Phosphatase enzyme (naturally present in raw milk) is completely destroyed by pasteurization — hence the Phosphatase test is used to detect inadequacy of pasteurization.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 63°C / 30 min → LTLT method, not HTST.
  • 72°C / 7 sec → Incorrect time; HTST requires 15 seconds at 72°C.
  • 74°C / 7 sec → That is Stassanization, not HTST.

posts.post_title: Milk Tests and Pasteurization Methods Match
posts.post_content:
Match the column:

TABLE-ITABLE-II
1. Coliform test(a) 72°C / 15 seconds
2. HTST(b) Mixing of cow & buffalo milk
3. Hansa test(c) 74°C / 7 seconds
4. Stassanization(d) Detergent adulteration of milk
5. Bromo-cresol-purple test(e) Faecal contamination of milk

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1-e, 2-a, 3-b, 4-c, 5-d
  • Coliform test (1-e): Indicates faecal contamination of milk (mainly E. coli — coliform bacteria originate from faecal matter).
  • HTST (2-a): High Temperature Short Time pasteurization — 72°C / 15 seconds.
  • Hansa test (3-b): Used to detect mixing of cow & buffalo milk.
  • Stassanization (4-c): A method of pasteurization at 74°C / 7 seconds.
  • Bromo-cresol-purple test (5-d): Used to detect detergent adulteration in milk.
Complete Quality Control Test Summary
  • Organoleptic test → Colour, flavour & taste
  • Coliform count test → Faecal contamination (E.coli)
  • Phosphatase test → Inadequacy of pasteurization
  • Hansa test → Mixing of cow & buffalo milk
  • Delvo kit test → Antibiotic & sulphur residues
  • Iodine solution → Starch adulteration
  • Picric acid → Gelatin adulteration
  • p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde → Urea adulteration
  • Bromo-cresol-purple → Detergent adulteration
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Option B: Swaps Coliform test and HTST.
  • Option C: Swaps Hansa test and Bromo-cresol-purple test.
  • Option D: Swaps HTST (72°C/15s) with Stassanization (74°C/7s).

posts.post_title: Maximum Plate Count for Pasteurized Milk
posts.post_content: Plate count for pasteurized milk should not exceed ________ per ml of milk:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 30,000 per ml

The Standard Plate Count (SPC) for pasteurized milk should not exceed 30,000 per ml. This is a regulatory limit to ensure adequate pasteurization and good quality milk reaches consumers.

Standard Plate Count Grades for Raw Milk
  • Less than 2 lakhs/ml: Very Good
  • 2–10 lakhs/ml: Good
  • 10–50 lakhs/ml: Fair
  • More than 50 lakhs/ml: Poor
For Pasteurized Milk

Pasteurized milk SPC ≤ 30,000 per ml — this ensures that pasteurization was effective and post-pasteurization contamination is minimal.

Methylene Blue Reduction Test Grades
  • 5 hours or more → Very Good
  • 3–4 hours → Good
  • 1–2 hours → Fair
  • 0.5 hour or less → Poor
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 50,000 → exceeds the acceptable limit for pasteurized milk.
  • 1 Lakh & 2 Lakhs → these are limits for raw milk quality grading (raw milk grades), not pasteurized milk.

posts.post_title: Preferred Milk for Khoa Making
posts.post_content: Which milk is always preferred for Khoa making?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Buffalo milk

Buffalo milk is always preferred for Khoa making due to its higher fat (5–6.6%) and total solids content, which gives better yield, richer texture, and superior flavour compared to cow milk.

Why Buffalo Milk is Preferred for Khoa
  • Higher fat content → richer, more palatable khoa.
  • Higher total solids → better yield per litre of milk.
  • Yield: 17–19% from cow milk vs. 21–23% from buffalo milk.
  • A minimum fat level of 4% in cow milk & 5% in buffalo milk is necessary for good quality khoa.
  • Khoa from buffalo milk contains 37.1% fat (cow milk khoa: 25.7% fat).
Khoa vs. Channa — Different Preferred Milk
  • Khoa: Buffalo milk preferred (more fat = better texture).
  • Channa: Cattle (Cow) milk preferred — cow milk channa has better quality due to coagulation properties of cow milk proteins and lower fat content allowing better drainage.
Classification of Khoa Products
  • Pindi Khoa → Burfi, Peda
  • Dhap Khoa → Gulabjamun, Pantooa
  • Danedar Khoa → Kalakand, Gourd barfi

posts.post_title: Colour of Milk from Grass-fed Cattle
posts.post_content: Grass-fed cattle yield milk of which colour?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Yellow colour milk

Grass-fed cattle yield yellow-coloured milk because fresh green grass is very rich in β-carotene. Cattle cannot fully convert β-carotene to Vitamin A, so the excess carotene passes into the milk fat, giving it a distinct yellow colour.

Key Contrast
  • Grass-fed cattle → Yellow milk (high β-carotene)
  • Stall-fed cattle → White-yellowish milk (moderate carotene from stored feed)
  • Buffalo → Pure white milk (complete carotene → Vitamin A conversion; zero residual carotene)
The Responsible Factor

The colour of milk fat = determined by its β-carotene (Carotene) content. Riboflavin is NOT responsible for yellow colour of milk fat (it causes the greenish-yellow colour of whey).

posts.post_title: Most Constant Physical Property of Milk
posts.post_content: The most constant physical property of milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Freezing point

The freezing point is the most constant (stable) physical property of milk. It remains nearly unchanged regardless of breed, season, or feed, making it the best indicator of water adulteration.

Freezing Point of Milk
  • Cow or Buffalo milk: −0.535°C to −0.550°C (average: −0.545°C)
  • Average depression of cow milk: −0.547°C; buffalo milk: −0.549°C
  • Lactose and chloride are primarily responsible for depressing the freezing point.
  • Addition of 1% water raises freezing point by 0.006°C.
  • Measured by: Hortvet cryoscope
Why Freezing Point is Used to Detect Water Adulteration

Since it is so constant, even a small addition of water (which has a freezing point of 0°C) raises the freezing point measurably, making it the best test for detecting water adulteration.

posts.post_title: Most Commercially Important Constituent of Milk
posts.post_content: The most commercially important constituent of milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fat

Fat is the most commercially important constituent of milk. Milk fat has the highest economic value and is the basis for pricing milk in many countries.

Importance of Milk Fat
  • Basis for market price of milk (fat-based payment systems)
  • Used to make high-value products: Butter, Ghee, Cream, Ice cream
  • Contains fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K
  • Provides characteristic flavour, texture and mouthfeel to dairy products
Milk Fat Facts
  • Most commercially important: Fat ✔
  • Most variable component: Fat
  • Most constant/least variable component: Lactose
  • Fat present in milk as: Emulsion (Fat-in-Water type)

posts.post_title: Teat Pairs in Bitch, Sow and Mare
posts.post_content: Pairs of teats present in bitch, sow, and mare respectively are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 5 pairs, 7 pairs & 1 pair

The number of teat pairs in different animals: Bitch = 5 pairs, Sow = 7 pairs, Mare = 1 pair.

Teat Numbers and Streak Canals in Different Animals
AnimalNo. of Teat PairsStreak Canals per Teat
Cattle, Buffalo2 pairs1
Sheep, Goat1 pair1
Camel2 pairs—
Bitch5 pairs8–14
Mare1 pair2
Sow7 pairs2
Memory Aid
  • Bitch: 5 pairs (10 teats) — supports large litters of puppies.
  • Sow: 7 pairs (14 teats) — supports the largest litter sizes among domestic animals.
  • Mare: 1 pair (2 teats) — mares typically have only one foal at a time.
  • Animal having two streak canals per teat: Mare and Sow.

posts.post_title: Why Milk Can Be Drawn Anytime from Goats
posts.post_content: Why can we draw milk at any time from a goat without a letdown stimulus?

_aimcq_options.text: Oxytocin reflex is not required in goat for letdown AND goat stores up to 80% of milk in the cisterns
Oxytocin reflex is not required in goat for letdown only
Goat stores up to 80% of milk in the alveoli
Goat has a unique type of teat canal that remains always open

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Oxytocin reflex is not required in goat for letdown AND goat stores up to 80% of milk in the cisterns

Both reasons together explain why milk can be drawn from goats at any time: (1) No oxytocin reflex is required for letdown in goats, and (2) Goats store up to 80% of their milk in the cisternal fraction — which is freely available without hormonal stimulation.

Milk Storage Proportions (Cistern:Alveolus)
  • Goat: 80:20 — most milk is in the cistern (freely available).
  • Sheep: 50:50
  • Cattle: 30:70
  • Buffalo & Camel: 5:95
  • Sow: 0:100 (all in alveoli)
Letdown Mechanism
  • In most animals, milk ejection requires oxytocin release (triggered by suckling or milking stimulus), which causes myoepithelial cell contraction around alveoli → milk moves into cisterns and ducts.
  • In goats, this reflex is largely bypassed because most milk is already stored in the cistern and can be expressed freely at any time.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Oxytocin reflex not required only → incomplete; the cistern storage is the primary structural reason.
  • Stores 80% in alveoli → opposite of the truth; it is 80% in cisterns.
  • Always-open teat canal → not a documented anatomical feature.

posts.post_title: Most Common Adulterant in Milk
posts.post_content: The most commonly used adulterant in milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Water

Water is the most commonly used adulterant in milk because it is cheap, easily available, and difficult to detect visually.

Detection of Water Adulteration
  • Best method: Freezing point depression test (Cryoscopy) — addition of 1% water raises the freezing point by 0.006°C (pure milk freezing point: −0.535°C to −0.550°C).
  • Lactometer reading (Specific gravity) also falls when water is added — because water has a lower density than milk.
Other Common Adulterants & Their Detection
  • Urea: detected by p-dimethylamino benzaldehyde reagent
  • Starch: detected by Iodine solution test (turns blue)
  • Detergent: detected by Bromo-cresol-purple solution
  • Gelatin: detected by Picric acid solution
  • Vanaspati (hydrogenated vegetable oil): detected by Baudoin test
  • Antibiotic residues: detected by Delvo kit test
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Urea, Detergent, Starch — while these are used as adulterants, water is by far the most commonly and frequently used adulterant in milk at the commercial level.

posts.post_title: Milk Constituents and Their Properties Match
posts.post_content:

2. Lactic acid(b) Sourness of milk

Correct Answer: 1-e, 2-a, 3-b, 4-c, 5-d

  • Lactic acid (2-a): Responsible for the real (true) acidity of milk. Lactic acid is formed by bacterial fermentation of lactose.
  • Volatile acids (3-b): Responsible for the sourness of milk (perceived sour taste from short-chain fatty acids produced during fermentation/rancidity).
  • β-Carotene (4-c): Responsible for the yellow colour of cow milk. Cow cannot fully convert all β-carotene to Vitamin A, so it accumulates in milk fat, giving a yellow tint. Buffalo efficiently converts carotene → Vitamin A, so buffalo milk is white.
  • Chloride (5-d): Responsible for the bitterness/saltiness of milk. Mastitis milk is high in chloride, making it bitter/salty.

  • Typical taste of milk → Lactose & Chloride together
  • Greenish-yellow colour of whey → Riboflavin
  • Bluish colour of skim milk → Riboflavin (after fat removal)
  • Flavouring agent in butter → Diacetyl (≤4 ppm)

posts.post_title: Colostrum Feeding in Calves
posts.post_content: Which is true about colostrum feeding in calf?

_aimcq_options.text: Colostrum provides passive immunity to the calf only
Colostrum is fed @ 10% of its body weight daily only
Colostrum acts as laxative & clears meconium only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above

All three statements about colostrum feeding are correct:

  1. Colostrum provides passive immunity: In ruminants (cow, buffalo), placental transfer of antibodies (immunoglobulins) does NOT occur due to the syndesmochorial type of placenta. So the calf is born with no antibodies and entirely depends on colostrum for passive immunity. Predominant Ig in bovine colostrum is IgG.
  2. Fed @ 10% of body weight daily: Colostrum is fed at 10% of the calf's body weight (approximately 2–2.5 liters/day) for the first 3–4 days after birth.
  3. Acts as laxative & clears meconium: Meconium is the first dark tarry faeces of the newborn calf. Colostrum has mild laxative properties due to high magnesium content, helping to expel meconium and establish normal gut function.
Additional Facts About Colostrum
  • Contains trypsin inhibitor → protects immunoglobulins from digestion in GIT.
  • Contains 5–15 times more Vitamin A than normal milk.
  • Milk loses colostral properties within 72 hours (3 days) after calving.
  • Colostrum specific gravity: 1.070 (much higher than normal milk at 1.028–1.032).

posts.post_title: Preferred Milk for Channa Making
posts.post_content: Which milk is best for Channa making?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cattle milk

Cattle (cow) milk is best for Channa making. Cow milk curdles more easily during acid coagulation due to its protein composition, producing a softer, smoother Channa with better functional properties.

What is Channa?
  • Channa is obtained by acid coagulation of hot milk followed by drainage of whey.
  • It is the base ingredient for Indian sweets like Rasogolla, Sandesh, Chum-chum, Ras-malai, Raj-bhog.
Why Buffalo Milk is Not Preferred
  • Buffalo milk has higher fat and casein content, producing a tougher, grainier curd that does not bind well for making Rasogolla or Sandesh.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Camel and Goat milk — not used for commercial Channa production.
  • Buffalo milk — preferred for Khoa, not Channa.

_aimcq_options.text: All of the above (Colour, Flavour, and Taste of milk)

Correct Answer: All of the above

The Organoleptic test evaluates milk quality using the five senses — it assesses colour, flavour (smell), and taste of milk simultaneously.

Quality Control Tests for Milk
  • Organoleptic test: Colour, flavour & taste
  • Hansa test: Mixing of cow & buffalo milk
  • Lactometer reading / Freezing point test: Adulteration with water
  • Coliform count test: Faecal contamination
  • COB (Clot-on-Boiling) test: Heat stability of milk
  • Phosphatase test: Inadequacy of pasteurization
  • Methylene blue reduction test / Resazurin test: Bacterial contamination

posts.post_title: Specific Gravity of Buffalo Milk
posts.post_content: The specific gravity of cow milk is 1.028–1.030, while that of buffalo milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1.030 to 1.032

The specific gravity of buffalo milk is 1.030–1.032, which is slightly higher than cow milk (1.028–1.030) due to its higher SNF and total solids content.

Specific Gravity of Different Milks
  • Cow milk: 1.028–1.030
  • Buffalo milk: 1.030–1.032
  • Skim milk: 1.035–1.037
  • Colostrum: 1.070
How Specific Gravity Changes
  • Decreases: Addition of water OR addition of cream/fat
  • Increases: Addition of skim milk OR removal of cream/fat
  • Formula: Specific gravity = 1 + CLR/1000 (CLR = Corrected Lactometer Reading)

posts.post_title: Boiling Point of Milk
posts.post_content: The boiling point of milk ranges from:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 100–101°C

The boiling point of milk ranges from 100°C to 101°C (average ~100.5°C), which is slightly higher than that of pure water (100°C at sea level), due to the dissolved solutes in milk.

Physical Properties of Milk — Key Values
  • Boiling point: 100–101°C (average 100.5°C) ✔
  • Freezing point: −0.535°C to −0.550°C
  • Melting point of milk fat: 33–35.5°C
  • Specific gravity (cow): 1.028–1.030
  • pH of cow milk: 6.4–6.6
Recknagel Phenomenon

The specific gravity of freshly drawn milk is low and increases by 0.001 as time advances — this is known as the Recknagel phenomenon.

posts.post_title: Pigment Responsible for Colour of Whey and Skim Milk
posts.post_content: Greenish-yellow colour of whey and bluish colour of skim milk is due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Riboflavin

Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) is a water-soluble, greenish-yellow fluorescent pigment. It remains in the aqueous (whey/serum) fraction of milk and is responsible for the greenish-yellow colour of whey. In skim milk (where fat and carotene are removed), the riboflavin gives a bluish tint.

Colour-Causing Pigments in Milk and Dairy Products
  • Riboflavin: Greenish-yellow colour of whey; bluish colour of skim milk.
  • β-Carotene: Yellow colour of cow milk and cow butter (carotene from green feed/grass).
  • Casein protein: White colour of buffalo milk (buffaloes convert all carotene to Vitamin A, so no carotene in their milk).
  • Annatto: Colouring agent added to butter to give it a yellow colour; also used as a food colour in cheese.
Stall-fed vs. Grass-fed Cattle Milk Colour
  • Stall-fed cow: White-yellowish milk (less carotene in feed).
  • Grass-fed cow: Yellow colour milk (more carotene from green pasture).

posts.post_title: Whole Milk Feeding Duration for Calf
posts.post_content: For proper growth of calf, whole milk feeding is desired up to the age of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 90 days

For proper growth and development of the calf, whole milk feeding is desired up to 90 days (3 months) of age. During this period, the calf's digestive system is not fully mature enough to effectively utilize solid feed.

Calf Feeding Protocol
  • Day 1–3/4: Colostrum feeding @ 10% of body weight per day (2–2.5 liters/day).
  • Day 4 onwards: Whole milk @ 10% of body weight.
  • Up to 90 days: Whole milk is the primary feed.
  • Creep feeding (calf starter / concentrate) can be introduced from 2–3 weeks of age alongside milk.
Importance of Colostrum (First 3–4 Days)
  • Provides passive immunity (immunoglobulins — mainly IgG in ruminants).
  • Acts as a laxative and clears meconium (first faeces of the newborn calf).
  • Contains trypsin inhibitor that protects immunoglobulins from digestion in GIT.
  • Contains 5–15 times more Vitamin A than normal milk.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 60 days — too short a period for complete rumen development and transition to solid feed.
  • 120 / 160 days — unnecessarily long; economically unviable and not required for proper calf growth.

posts.post_title: True Statements About Khoa
posts.post_content: Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about khoa?

_aimcq_options.text: It is concentrated whole milk product only
Khoa of cow milk contains 103 ppm iron only
Danedar khoa is used to make kalakand only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above

All three statements about Khoa are correct:

  1. It is a concentrated whole milk product — Khoa (also called Mawa) is made by heat-desiccation (partial dehydration) of whole milk in an iron karahi (wok).
  2. Khoa of cow milk contains 103 ppm iron — Normal milk contains only 2–4 ppm iron. The high iron content of khoa is because it is prepared in an iron karahi, which leaches iron into the product.
  3. Danedar Khoa is used to make Kalakand — Milk of high acidity produces granular (danedar) texture khoa, ideal for Kalakand and Gourd barfi.
Classification of Khoa
  • Pindi Khoa (21–26% fat): Used for Burfi, Peda
  • Dhap Khoa (20–23% fat): Used for Gulabjamun, Pantooa
  • Danedar Khoa (20–25% fat): Used for Kalakand, Gourd barfi
Preferred Milk for Khoa

Buffalo milk is preferred for khoa making because of its higher fat content (5%) and higher total solids, giving better yield and texture. Yield: 17–19% from cow milk and 21–23% from buffalo milk.

posts.post_title: Calculating Specific Gravity from CLR
posts.post_content: If CLR (Corrected Lactometer Reading) of milk is 28, find out the specific gravity of milk:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1.028

Using the formula: Specific gravity of milk = 1 + CLR/1000

Given CLR = 28:

Specific gravity = 1 + 28/1000 = 1 + 0.028 = 1.028

Why This Formula?

The Quevenne Lactometer reads directly in CLR units (graduated 15 to 40 on the scale). To convert to the actual specific gravity (density relative to water), you use: SG = 1 + CLR/1000.

Normal Specific Gravity Values
  • Cow milk: 1.028–1.030 (CLR 28–30)
  • Buffalo milk: 1.030–1.032 (CLR 30–32)
  • Skim milk: 1.035–1.037 (CLR 35–37)
  • Colostrum: ~1.070
  • Water: 1.000
Effect on Specific Gravity
  • Addition of water OR addition of fat/cream: Decreases specific gravity (dilutes the denser constituents).
  • Addition of skim milk OR removal of fat: Increases specific gravity.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 1.025 → CLR of 25; not the result for CLR 28.
  • 0.28 → omits adding 1 to CLR/1000; wrong application of formula.
  • 1.28 → divides CLR by 100 instead of 1000; incorrect formula application.

posts.post_title: Product Obtained by Acid Coagulation of Hot Milk
posts.post_content: The product obtained by acid coagulation of hot milk and subsequent drainage of whey is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Channa

Channa is the product obtained by acid coagulation of hot milk and subsequent drainage of whey. It is a fresh, unripened coagulated milk product widely used in Indian sweets.

How Channa is Made
  • Hot milk (just below boiling) is curdled by adding an acid — citric acid, lactic acid, or dilute acetic acid.
  • The curds (coagulum) are separated from whey by draining through muslin cloth.
  • The resulting soft, moist curd is Channa.
Uses of Channa
  • Base & filler for: Rasogolla, Sandesh, Chum-chum, Ras-malai, Raj-bhog
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Khoa — made by partial dehydration (evaporation) of whole milk, not acid coagulation.
  • Paneer — made similarly to Channa but pressed into a firm block.
  • Rasogolla — a sweet prepared FROM Channa, not from acid coagulation itself.

posts.post_title: Hormone Responsible for Milk Hold-Up
posts.post_content: The hormone responsible for holding up of milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Epinephrine (Adrenaline)

Epinephrine (Adrenaline) is the hormone responsible for holding up of milk (milk inhibition/suppression of milk let-down). It is released during stress, fear, or excitement and causes vasoconstriction of udder blood vessels, preventing oxytocin from reaching the myoepithelial cells.

Contrast: Oxytocin vs. Epinephrine
  • Oxytocin: The milk let-down hormone — it causes contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding alveoli, pushing milk into cisterns and ducts.
  • Epinephrine: The milk hold-up hormone — antagonizes oxytocin action; released during stress/pain/fear.
Practical Implication

This is why milking should be done in a calm, stress-free environment. Any disturbance (loud noise, pain, new milker) causes epinephrine release and the cow withholds milk — even if she has been milked partially.

Residual Milk

Residual milk (milk left in udder after normal milking) can only be obtained after oxytocin injection or by re-milking.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Oxytocin → causes milk let-down (opposite function).
  • Vasopressin → antidiuretic hormone; not directly related to milk ejection.
  • Calcitonin → regulates calcium metabolism; not involved in milk ejection reflex.

posts.post_title: Factors Decreasing Specific Gravity of Milk
posts.post_content: The specific gravity of milk is decreased by:

_aimcq_options.text: Both addition of water and addition of fat

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both addition of water and addition of fat

The specific gravity (SG) of milk is decreased by:

  1. Addition of water: Water (SG = 1.000) has lower density than milk (SG ~1.028–1.032), so adding water dilutes milk and lowers its SG. This is the basis for detecting water adulteration.
  2. Addition of fat/cream: Milk fat has SG of about 0.93 (less than 1), so adding cream or fat lowers the overall SG of milk.
Factors Increasing Specific Gravity
  • Addition of skim milk: Skim milk (SG 1.035–1.037) has higher SG than whole milk, so adding it increases SG.
  • Removal of fat/cream: Removing the lower-density fat fraction increases overall SG — that's why skim milk has higher SG than whole milk.
Recknagel Phenomenon

The specific gravity of freshly drawn milk is low — it increases by about 0.001 as time advances. This is because dissolved gases escape and fat globule distribution stabilizes after milking.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Addition of water only → correct but incomplete; fat also decreases SG.
  • Addition of fat only → correct but incomplete; water also decreases SG.
  • Addition of skim milk → this actually INCREASES specific gravity, not decreases it.

  • Lecithin (a phospholipid) is the excellent emulsifying agent that stabilizes the milk fat emulsion.
  • Other phospholipids: Cephalin, Sphingomyelin.
Memory Aid
  • Milk/Cream = fat globules floating in water → Fat-in-Water
  • Butter = water droplets trapped inside fat → Water-in-Fat (phase inversion during churning)

posts.post_title: Most Variable Component of Milk
posts.post_content: The most variable component of milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fat

Fat is the most variable component of milk. Its content fluctuates widely depending on several factors.

Factors Affecting Milk Fat %
  • Breed: Buffalo milk (6.6%) has far more fat than cow milk (4.6%).
  • Stage of lactation: Fat % is higher in colostrum and at the end of lactation.
  • Time of milking: Evening milk has higher fat than morning milk.
  • Order of milking: Final stripping has much higher fat % than foremilk.
  • Feeding: Stall-fed cows give white-yellowish milk; grass-fed give yellow-coloured milk.
  • Yield: High-yielding breeds tend to have lower fat %.
Least Variable Component

Lactose is the least variable component of milk. It is synthesized in the mammary gland and its production is tightly regulated, making it the most consistent constituent across breeds and conditions.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Lactose → least variable, not most variable.
  • Casein → relatively stable but more variable than lactose; still not the most variable.
  • SNF → includes fat-free solids; though SNF itself is more stable, fat variation dominates the total solids picture.

posts.post_title: Type of Fermentation in Kefir and Kumiss
posts.post_content: Kefir & Kumiss are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lactic acid-alcohol fermented milk

Both Kefir and Kumiss are lactic acid-alcohol fermented milk beverages — they undergo dual fermentation producing both lactic acid and alcohol (ethanol), making them mildly alcoholic dairy drinks.

Kefir
  • Self-carbonated milk beverage containing 1% lactic acid & 1% alcohol.
  • Fermenting agents are called Kefir grains — containing Streptococcus lactis, Kefir bacilli & lactose-fermenting yeast.
  • Kefir is the self-carbonated beverage (note: Kumiss is also carbonated).
Kumiss
  • Originally prepared from Mare's milk only.
  • Fermented by Lactobacillus acidophilus.
  • Finished product contains 2.5% alcohol (higher than Kefir).
  • Alcohol content: Kefir = 1%; Kumiss = 2.5%.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Acetic acid-alcohol → this describes vinegar fermentation; not applicable to Kefir/Kumiss.
  • Lactic acid-phenol → phenol is not a fermentation product; this is a fabricated distractor.
  • Lactic acid-acetic acid → describes mixed acid fermentation; no significant alcohol produced.

posts.post_title: Fat Globule Size in Homogenized Milk
posts.post_content: The size of fat globule in homogenized milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 2 µm

After homogenization, the fat globule size in milk is reduced to 2 micrometres (2 µm) or less. This makes the emulsion extremely stable and prevents cream from rising to the top.

Homogenization

Homogenization is the process of making a stable emulsion of milk serum and milk fat by forcing milk through a tiny orifice under high pressure (homogenizer). This breaks large fat globules into uniformly small ones.

Effects of Homogenization
  • Fat globule size reduced to ≤2 µm (from normal 2–5 µm).
  • Cream does NOT rise (no cream line) — stable emulsion.
  • Viscosity increases after homogenization (more surface area of fat globules).
  • Cannot separate cream from homogenized milk by gravity.
  • Milk appears whiter due to greater light scattering by smaller globules.
  • More digestible — smaller fat globules are easier to digest.
Normal Fat Globule Size

In normal (non-homogenized) milk: average 2–5 µm; range 0–10 µm.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 3, 4, 5 µm → these are within the normal (pre-homogenization) range. After homogenization, size is specifically reduced to 2 µm or below.

_aimcq_options.text: All of the above (Kefir, Kumiss, Dahi, Lassi, Srikhand)

Correct Answer: All of the above

All the listed items — Kefir, Kumiss, Dahi, Lassi, and Srikhand — are fermented dairy products.

Types of Fermented Dairy Products
  • Kefir — lactic acid + alcohol fermented milk (1% lactic acid, 1% alcohol); self-carbonated beverage fermented by Kefir grains (Str. lactis, Kefir bacilli, lactose-fermenting yeast).
  • Kumiss — lactic acid + alcohol fermented product from mare's milk; fermented by L. acidophilus; contains 2.5% alcohol.
  • Dahi — Indian curd; coagulated by lactic fermentation.
  • Lassi — Indian buttermilk; a by-product of dahi churning.
  • Srikhand — semi-soft, sweetish-sour fermented curd.

posts.post_title: Incorrect Statement About Milk Composition and Milking
posts.post_content: Which of the following statement is NOT true?

_aimcq_options.text: Evening milk contains lesser fat than morning milk
Final stripping contains higher fat than fore-milk
Bacterial count is higher in foremilk than in final stripping
Morning milk contains lesser fat than evening milk

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Evening milk contains lesser fat than morning milk

This statement is NOT true. In reality, evening milk contains HIGHER fat than morning milk. The cow is milked less frequently at night, so the milk accumulates for a longer period and has higher fat content.

Correct Facts About Milk Composition
  • Final stripping contains higher fat than fore-milk ✔ — fat content increases progressively during milking; last milk drawn (stripping) is richest in fat.
  • Bacterial count is higher in foremilk than in final stripping ✔ — fore-milk (first few strips) contains more bacteria from the teat canal; hence it should not be mixed with the rest of the milk.
  • Evening milk > Morning milk in fat ✔ — longer inter-milking interval at night → more fat accumulation.

posts.post_title: Form in Which Casein Exists in Milk
posts.post_content: Casein exists in milk in the form of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Calcium-caseinate-phosphate complex

Casein exists in milk in the form of a Calcium-caseinate-phosphate complex (also called a casein micelle). This complex provides stability to casein in milk.

Casein — Key Facts
  • Constitutes about 80% of total milk protein
  • Cow milk: 3% casein | Buffalo milk: 4.3% casein
  • Responsible for the white colour and viscosity of milk
  • Present in milk as a colloidal suspension
  • Types: α-casein (αs-casein + K-casein), β-casein, γ-casein
Casein Subtypes
  • αs-casein: Calcium-sensitive; precipitated by calcium ions
  • K-casein: Calcium-insensitive; NOT precipitated by calcium ions; stabilizes the casein micelle

posts.post_title: Effect of Temperature on Milk Viscosity
posts.post_content: With an increase in the temperature of milk, its viscosity will:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Decrease

With an increase in temperature, the viscosity of milk decreases. This is consistent with the general behaviour of liquids — as temperature rises, molecular movement increases and intermolecular friction decreases, leading to reduced viscosity.

Viscosity of Milk — Key Values
  • Viscosity of whole milk at 25°C: approximately 2.0 centipoise
  • Viscosity of skim milk at 25°C: approximately 1.5 centipoise
Factors Affecting Milk Viscosity
  • Temperature ↑ → Viscosity ↓ (inverse relationship)
  • Homogenization → Viscosity ↑ (fat globule surface area increases, more friction)
  • Fat content ↑ → Viscosity ↑
  • Casein protein is primarily responsible for the viscosity and white colour of milk.
Remember the Contrast
  • Temperature increase → viscosity decreases
  • Homogenization → viscosity increases

posts.post_title: Type of Emulsion in Butter
posts.post_content: Butter is which type of emulsion?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Water in fat

Butter is a water-in-fat (W/O) emulsion — tiny water droplets are dispersed within a continuous fat phase. This is the opposite of milk (fat-in-water).

Phase Inversion During Butter Making
  • When cream (fat-in-water) is churned, a phase inversion occurs.
  • The fat globule membrane breaks, fat globules clump together, and small water droplets become trapped within the fat mass.
  • This converts the fat-in-water emulsion of cream into the water-in-fat emulsion of butter.
Composition of Butter
  • Contains all fat-soluble vitamins: Vitamin A, D, E, and K.
  • Flavouring agent: Diacetyl (≤4 ppm).
  • Yellow colour: Due to Annatto (added colouring agent).
  • Fishy odour in butter: Due to rancidity.
  • Best method of ghee making: Pre-stratification method.
Emulsion Summary
  • Milk, Cream → Fat in water (O/W)
  • Butter → Water in fat (W/O)

posts.post_title: Instrument to Measure Milk Fat

Gerber's Butyrometer is used to measure the fat content of milk. It is the best and most widely used method for fat estimation (Gerber method).

Other Methods for Fat Estimation
  • Soxhlet apparatus: used for accurate fat extraction in laboratory; solvent extraction method.
  • Rose-Gottlieb method: another laboratory reference method for fat determination.
Other Instruments and Their Uses
  • Quevenne Lactometer: measures specific gravity of milk (at 15.6°C).
  • Hydrometer / Pycnometer: measures density of milk (at 20°C).
  • Hortvet Cryoscope: measures freezing point of milk.
  • Zeiss Refractometer: measures refractive index of milk (at 20°C).
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Lactometer → measures specific gravity, not fat %.
  • Pycnometer → measures density, not fat %.
  • Hortvet apparatus → measures freezing point of milk, not fat %.

posts.post_title: Fortified and Irradiated Milk
posts.post_content: Which of the following pair is correctly matched regarding special types of milk?

_aimcq_options.text: Both: Fortified milk is Mineralized & Vitaminized milk; Irradiated milk – Vitamin D content increased by UV exposure
Fortified milk only – Mineralized & Vitaminized milk
Irradiated milk only – Vitamin D content increased by UV exposure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both statements are correct
  1. Fortified milk: Milk that has been enriched with added minerals and/or vitamins beyond its natural content — hence called Mineralized & Vitaminized milk. Example: Vitamin D-fortified milk, calcium-fortified milk.
  2. Irradiated milk: Milk exposed to UV rays, which converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in milk fat into Vitamin D (cholecalciferol). This increases the Vitamin D content of milk without adding any chemical supplements.
Key Vitamins and Milk Processing
  • Vitamin D: Increased by UV irradiation (irradiated milk).
  • Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) & Vitamin C: Lost/destroyed during pasteurization and sterilization.
  • Butter: Contains all fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).
  • Cow milk: Particularly rich in Vitamin A and carotene.
  • Milk: Good source of thiamine and riboflavin; poor source of Vitamin C.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Options B and C are individually correct but incomplete — since both pairs are correctly matched, 'Both' is the right answer.

posts.post_title: Self-Carbonated Milk Beverage
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a self-carbonated milk beverage?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Kefir

Kefir is specifically described as a self-carbonated milk beverage. The CO₂ produced by the yeast component of Kefir grains during lactose fermentation creates natural carbonation within the beverage, giving it a slightly fizzy, effervescent character.

Why Kefir is Self-Carbonated

Kefir is made in a closed container. Yeast in the Kefir grains ferments lactose → ethanol + CO₂. Since the container is sealed, CO₂ is retained in the liquid, making it self-carbonated.

Comparison of Kefir and Kumiss
  • Kefir: Self-carbonated; 1% lactic acid + 1% alcohol; from any milk; uses Kefir grains.
  • Kumiss: Also slightly effervescent but not classically termed 'self-carbonated'; 2.5% alcohol; from mare's milk; fermented by L. acidophilus + yeast.

In the standard textbook definition (as per G.C. Banerjee, Animal Husbandry), Kefir alone is termed 'self-carbonated milk beverage.'

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Kumiss → not specifically termed 'self-carbonated' in standard references.
  • Both → Kumiss is not classically defined as a self-carbonated beverage.
  • None → Kefir is indeed self-carbonated.

posts.post_title: Method to Obtain Residual Milk
posts.post_content: Residual milk is obtained only after:

Residual milk is the amount of milk left in the udder after normal milking. It can be obtained only by:

  • Oxytocin injection — causes forceful milk ejection from alveoli
  • Re-milking — a second milking shortly after the first
Key Facts About Residual Milk

posts.post_title: Effect of Homogenization on Milk Viscosity
posts.post_content: After homogenization, the viscosity of milk will:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Increase

After homogenization, the viscosity of milk increases. Homogenization breaks down large fat globules into smaller ones (≤2 µm), dramatically increasing their total surface area. This means more fat–protein interaction, more resistance to flow, and thus higher viscosity.

Key Facts About Homogenization
  • Homogenization creates a stable emulsion of milk serum and milk fat using a homogenizer.
  • Fat globule size in homogenized milk: 2 microns (2 µm) (reduced from natural average of 2–5 µm).
  • After homogenization, cream cannot be separated from milk by gravity.
  • Viscosity increases because the increased surface area of smaller globules causes greater internal friction.
Contrast with Temperature Effect
  • Temperature ↑ → viscosity decreases
  • Homogenization → viscosity increases
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Decrease → opposite is true; homogenization always increases viscosity.
  • No change → the physical change in fat globule size directly affects viscosity.

posts.post_title: Facts About Kefir
posts.post_content: Which of the following is/are true about Kefir?

_aimcq_options.text: It is a self-carbonated milk beverage containing 1% lactic acid & 1% alcohol only
Fermenting agents for Kefir are known as Kefir grains only
Kefir grains contain Str. lactis, Kefir bacilli & lactose fermenting yeast only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above

All three statements about Kefir are correct:

  1. Self-carbonated milk beverage: Kefir is self-carbonated due to CO₂ produced by yeast fermentation. It contains 1% lactic acid (from bacterial fermentation) and 1% alcohol (from yeast fermentation of lactose).
  2. Kefir grains: The unique fermenting agents used in Kefir production. Kefir grains are irregular, rubbery, white/yellow granules containing a symbiotic community of microorganisms embedded in a polysaccharide-protein matrix.
  3. Microbial composition of Kefir grains: Contains Streptococcus lactis (lactic acid bacteria), Kefir bacilli (lactobacillus species), and lactose-fermenting yeasts. This mixed culture produces both lactic acid and alcohol simultaneously.
Kefir vs. Kumiss — Key Differences
  • Kefir: 1% alcohol; any milk; self-carbonated; uses Kefir grains.
  • Kumiss: 2.5% alcohol; originally only mare's milk; fermented by L. acidophilus.

posts.post_title: Alcohol Content of Kefir and Kumiss
posts.post_content: Alcohol content of Kefir & Kumiss are respectively:

Correct Answer: 1% (Kefir) & 2.5% (Kumiss)

Kefir contains 1% alcohol and 1% lactic acid. Kumiss contains 2.5% alcohol. Kumiss has approximately 2.5 times more alcohol than Kefir because mare's milk is richer in lactose (~6.2%) which provides more substrate for yeast fermentation.

Why Kumiss Has More Alcohol Than Kefir
  • Mare's milk has higher lactose content (~6.2%) compared to cow milk (~4.9%).
  • More lactose → more substrate for yeast → more ethanol produced.
  • Fermentation conditions and culture used (L. acidophilus + yeast) also favor higher alcohol production in Kumiss.
Fermented Dairy Products — Key Numerical Data
  • Kefir: 1% lactic acid + 1% alcohol
  • Kumiss: ~0.7–1% lactic acid + 2.5% alcohol
  • Dahi: 0.5–1% starter, fermented at room temperature
  • Srikhand: Minimum 8.5% fat, max 72.5% sugar (on dry basis)

The ideal inter-milking interval (time between two successive milkings) is 12 hours. This maintains a balance between milk accumulation and udder health.

Milking Schedule

  • Ideal vacuum for cattle: 352 mmHg; for buffalo: 400 mmHg

Irradiated milk is produced by exposing milk to UV rays, which converts the precursor 7-dehydrocholesterol (present in milk fat) into Vitamin D. This process is also called UV irradiation of milk.

  • Milk is a poor source of Vitamin C.

posts.post_title: Type of Lal Dahi from Eastern India

posts.post_title: Physical State of Fat in Milk
posts.post_content: Fat is present in milk as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Emulsion

Fat is present in milk as an Emulsion — specifically a fat-in-water (O/W) emulsion. Fat globules are dispersed in the aqueous phase of milk, stabilized by the fat globule membrane and the emulsifying agent Lecithin (a phospholipid).

Form of Different Milk Constituents in Milk
  • Fat: Emulsion (fat-in-water type)
  • Casein protein: Colloidal suspension (as calcium-caseinate-phosphate complex)
  • Whey proteins (α-lactalbumin & β-lactoglobulin): Colloidal solution
  • Lactose & Ash (minerals): True solution
Emulsion Types in Dairy
  • Milk & Cream: Fat-in-water (O/W) emulsion
  • Butter: Water-in-fat (W/O) emulsion

  • Normal milk: 2–5 µm

  • Solution → for lactose and minerals (true solution).
  • Suspension → for casein (colloidal suspension).

posts.post_title: Facts About Kumiss
posts.post_content: Which of the following is/are true about Kumiss?

_aimcq_options.text: Both: It is lactic acid-alcohol fermented from mare milk; fermented by L. acidophilus; finished product contains 2.5% alcohol
It is lactic acid-alcohol fermented milk obtained from mare milk only
It is fermented by Lactobacillus acidophilus & finished product contains 2.5% alcohol only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Both statements are true
  1. Kumiss is a lactic acid-alcohol fermented milk obtained from mare's milk: Kumiss originated in Central Asia among horse-herding nomads. It is traditionally prepared exclusively from mare's (female horse) milk, which is naturally higher in lactose (~6.2%) than cow milk, supporting greater alcohol production.
  2. Fermented by Lactobacillus acidophilus; finished product contains 2.5% alcohol: The fermentation is carried out by Lactobacillus acidophilus (lactic acid bacteria) and lactose-fermenting yeasts in combination, producing lactic acid and 2.5% ethanol in the finished product.

  • Kefir: Any milk; Kefir grains (mixed culture); 1% lactic acid + 1% alcohol; self-carbonated.
  • Kumiss: Mare's milk; L. acidophilus + yeast; lactic acid + 2.5% alcohol.

posts.post_title: Original Milk Used for Kumiss Preparation
posts.post_content: Kumiss is originally prepared only from:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mare milk

Kumiss is traditionally and originally prepared only from Mare's milk (milk of the female horse). It originated among the nomadic peoples of the Central Asian steppes (Kazakhstan, Mongolia) where horses were the primary livestock.

Why Mare's Milk is Used
  • Mare's milk has higher lactose content (~6.2%) than cow milk, providing more substrate for fermentation.
  • It produces a final product with 2.5% alcohol — higher than cow milk-based beverages.
  • Mare's milk also has a composition closer to human milk (low casein, high whey protein), making it particularly suitable for sensitive digestive systems.
Cultural Significance

Kumiss has been consumed for over 5,000 years. In Mongolian culture, it holds ceremonial importance (called 'Airag' in Mongolian). Modern adaptations use cow's milk but the traditional product uses only mare's milk.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Sheep milk → used for many traditional cheeses, not Kumiss.
  • Buffalo milk → used in India for many dairy products (khoa, paneer, ghee), not Kumiss.
  • Goat milk → used for goat cheese and some fermented milks, not Kumiss.

posts.post_title: Best Test for Detecting Water Adulteration in Milk
posts.post_content: Adulteration of milk with water is best judged by the determination of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Freezing point

The Freezing point depression test (Cryoscopy) using the Hortvet cryoscope is the best and most reliable method to detect water adulteration in milk. Pure milk has a constant freezing point of −0.535°C to −0.550°C (average −0.545°C). Addition of water raises (i.e., brings it closer to 0°C) this freezing point.

Why Freezing Point is the Best Test
  • The freezing point of milk is the most constant physical property of milk.
  • Addition of 1% water to milk raises its freezing point by 0.006°C.
  • The test is highly sensitive and cannot be easily manipulated by adding other solutes (which would alter other properties).
  • Note: Mastitis milk shows a normal freezing point (not depressed), because mastitis increases chloride which compensates for the drop in lactose.
Why Specific Gravity Alone is Not Best
  • Specific gravity can be manipulated by adding skim milk (raises SG) along with water (lowers SG), masking adulteration.
  • Freezing point is more specific and harder to falsify.
Instrument Used
  • Hortvet cryoscope / Hortvet apparatus — measures the freezing point of milk.

  • Natural preservatives in milk: Lactoperoxidase, Lactoferrin, Conglutinin

posts.post_title: Use of Hortvet Apparatus
posts.post_content: Hortvet apparatus is used to measure which physical property of milk?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Freezing point

Hortvet Cryoscope (Hortvet apparatus) is used to measure the freezing point of milk.

Freezing Point of Milk
  • Normal freezing point of milk: −0.535°C to −0.550°C (average −0.545°C)
  • Cow milk average: −0.547°C; Buffalo milk average: −0.549°C
  • Freezing point of pure distilled water: 0°C
  • Soluble constituents (mainly lactose and chloride) depress the freezing point below 0°C.
  • Addition of 1% water raises the freezing point by 0.006°C — making it the best test for water adulteration in milk.
Instruments and the Properties They Measure
  • Quevenne Lactometer (15.6°C): Specific gravity
  • Hydrometer / Pycnometer (20°C): Density
  • Zeiss Refractometer (20°C): Refractive index (normal: 1.344–1.348)
  • Hortvet Cryoscope: Freezing point ✔
  • Gerber's Butyrometer: Fat %
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Refractive index → measured by Zeiss refractometer.
  • Specific gravity → measured by Quevenne Lactometer.
  • Colour → assessed by organoleptic test, not Hortvet apparatus.

posts.post_title: Component Responsible for Viscosity and White Colour of Milk
posts.post_content: Viscosity and white colour of milk is due to:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Casein protein

Casein protein is primarily responsible for both the viscosity and white colour of milk. Casein exists as a colloidal suspension of large calcium-caseinate-phosphate micelles, which scatter visible light and give milk its characteristic white, opaque appearance.

How Casein Causes White Colour
  • Casein micelles are large enough (~20–300 nm) to scatter all wavelengths of visible light equally → milk appears white (Tyndall effect / Mie scattering).
  • Buffalo milk is white because buffalo efficiently converts all carotene → colourless Vitamin A, so no yellow pigment remains, and casein's white colour dominates.
  • Cow milk is slightly yellow due to residual β-carotene that is not fully converted to Vitamin A.
How Casein Affects Viscosity
  • The large casein micelles increase the internal resistance to flow → higher viscosity than water.
  • Normal whole milk viscosity at 25°C: ~1.5–2.0 centipoise.
  • Homogenization increases viscosity (smaller, more numerous fat globules increase surface area interactions).
  • Increasing temperature decreases milk viscosity.
Casein Facts
  • Constitutes ~80% of total milk protein.
  • Cow milk: 3% casein; Buffalo milk: 4.3% casein.
  • Exists as calcium-caseinate-phosphate complex.
  • Three types: α-casein (αs-casein = calcium-sensitive + K-casein = calcium-insensitive), β-casein, γ-casein.

  • Ice-cream — Western origin; made from pasteurized milk with whipping (has overrun); lighter, creamier texture.
Classification of Indian Dairy Products
  • Concentrated whole milk products: Kheer/Basundi, Khoa/Mawa, Rabri, Kulfi
  • Coagulated milk products: Dahi, Srikhand, Paneer, Channa
  • Clarified butterfat products: Makkhan, Ghee, Lassi

Correct Answer: Lactose and Chloride

Lactose and Chloride are primarily responsible for depressing the freezing point of milk below 0°C.

Why Freezing Point of Milk is Below 0°C
  • Pure water freezes at 0°C.
  • Milk has dissolved solutes (mainly lactose and chloride salts) which lower the freezing point through the colligative property of freezing point depression.
  • Freezing point of milk: −0.535°C to −0.550°C
Practical Application
  • Addition of 1% water raises the freezing point by 0.006°C.
  • Therefore, freezing point measurement is the best method to detect water adulteration.

posts.post_content: Cow milk proteins possess which of the following as compared to buffalo milk proteins?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: High digestibility & high biological value

Cow milk proteins have high digestibility and high biological value compared to buffalo milk proteins. This makes cow milk particularly suitable for infant feeding and clinical nutrition.

Biological Value of Milk Proteins
  • Biological value of cow milk: 86.90
  • Biological value of buffalo milk: 84.04
Essential Amino Acids in Milk Proteins
  • Milk proteins contain all essential amino acids in adequate amounts.
  • They are particularly rich in Lysine and Valine.
Milk Protein Classification

  • Whey proteins (milk serum proteins): α-lactalbumin and β-lactoglobulin; present as colloidal solution.

  • High digestibility & low BV → incorrect; cow milk has both high digestibility AND high BV.

posts.post_title: Material for Dairy Utensil Manufacturing
posts.post_content: The material mainly used for manufacturing dairy utensils is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Aluminum / Stainless steel

Aluminum and stainless steel are the materials mainly used for manufacturing dairy utensils. Stainless steel (SS 304 or SS 316) is the preferred material in modern dairies.

Why Stainless Steel and Aluminium?
  • Non-reactive with milk acids and cleaning agents.
  • Easy to clean and sanitize (smooth, non-porous surface).
  • Durable and resistant to corrosion.
  • Does not impart off-flavours or metallic taste to milk.
  • Meets food-grade safety standards.
Why Other Metals Are Avoided
  • Copper: Catalyzes oxidative rancidity in milk fat; causes off-flavours.
  • Iron: Rusts easily; iron contamination (though karahi/iron pans are used for khoa making, giving high iron content of 103 ppm).
  • Bronze: Contains copper — same issues as copper.

posts.post_title: Dry Matter Percentage of Sow Milk
posts.post_content: Dry matter percentage of sow milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 10%

Sow (female pig) milk has a water content of approximately 89.6%, which means its dry matter (total solids) percentage is approximately 10.4% ≈ 10%.

Dry Matter of Different Animal Milks
  • Sow milk: ~10% dry matter (water ~90%)
  • Cow milk: ~13% dry matter (water ~87%)
  • Buffalo milk: ~15.8% dry matter (water ~84%)
  • Sheep milk: ~20.6% dry matter (water ~79%)
Sow Milk Special Feature

Sow milk has a unique characteristic — 100% of milk is stored in alveoli (0% in cisterns). This means piglets must continuously stimulate the teat for milk let-down; they cannot draw milk at will like goat kids. This is why sows nurse their piglets many times per day in short bursts.

  • 17% → not a standard value for any common species milk.

  • Whey protein nitrogen: ~15% of total N (α-lactalbumin, β-lactoglobulin)

posts.post_title: Duration for Milk to Lose Colostral Properties
posts.post_content: Milk loses its colostral properties and becomes normal within how many hours after calving?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 72 hours

Milk loses its colostral properties and becomes normal within 72 hours (3–4 days) after calving. During this period, the composition gradually shifts from colostrum (high protein/immunoglobulin, low lactose) to normal whole milk.

Colostrum — Key Characteristics
  • Fed to newborn calf @ 10% of its body weight per day (or 2–2.5 litres/day) for the first 3–4 days.
  • Contains a trypsin inhibitor that protects immunoglobulins from digestion in the GIT of the calf.
  • Provides passive immunity to the calf (placental transfer of antibodies does not occur in ruminants).
  • Acts as a laxative, clearing meconium (first faeces of the newborn).
  • Contains 5–15 times more Vitamin A than normal milk.
  • Predominant immunoglobulin: IgG in bovine colostrum; IgA in human colostrum.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 48 hours → too short; colostral properties persist for 72 hours (3–4 days).
  • 24 hours → only 1 day; colostrum is fed and remains effective up to 3–4 days.
  • 96 hours → slightly longer than the standard 72-hour reference.

posts.post_title: Heart of the Milking Machine
posts.post_content: Which component of the milking machine is known as the 'heart of the milking machine'?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pulsator

The pulsator is known as the 'heart of the milking machine'. It creates alternating vacuum and atmospheric pressure cycles that simulate the suckling action and massage the teats.

Functions of a Milking Machine
  • Opens the streak canal with partial vacuum → allows continuous milk flow.
  • Massages the teats → prevents congestion of blood in the teat.
Key Milking Machine Parameters
  • Pulsation rate: Optimum = 60 cycles/minute (not <40 or >120 cycles/min).
  • Pulsation ratio: Cattle = 60/40; Buffalo = 50/50.
  • Ideal vacuum: Cattle = 352 mmHg; Buffalo = 400 mmHg.
  • Recommended vacuum: 10–15 inches of mercury.
  • Minimum herd size for machine milking: 20 animals.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Vacuum pump → creates and maintains the overall vacuum; important but not called the 'heart'.
  • Regulator → controls vacuum pressure; a supporting component.
  • Teat cup shell → physical interface between the machine and the cow's teat.

posts.post_title: Physical State of Lactose and Ash in Milk
posts.post_content: Lactose & ash present in milk as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: True Solution

Both Lactose (milk sugar) and Ash (minerals/salts) are present in milk as a True Solution — they are completely dissolved in the aqueous phase of milk at molecular or ionic level.

Physical States of Milk Constituents
  • Fat: Emulsion (fat-in-water type O/W emulsion)
  • Casein protein: Colloidal suspension (as calcium-caseinate-phosphate complex)
  • Whey proteins (α-lactalbumin, β-lactoglobulin): Colloidal solution
  • Lactose & Ash: True solution ✔
Significance of True Solution Form

Because lactose and minerals are in true solution, they are osmotically active and are primarily responsible for depressing the freezing point of milk below 0°C. Specifically, lactose and chloride are the main contributors to freezing point depression (FPD).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Emulsion → for fat.
  • Suspension → for casein (colloidal suspension).
  • Colloidal suspension → for casein protein specifically.

posts.post_title: Lactose Content of Cow and Buffalo Milk
posts.post_content: Average lactose content of cow milk & buffalo milk respectively is:

Correct Answer: 4.9% (Cow) & 5.2% (Buffalo)

  • Buffalo milk: 5.2%
  • Goat milk: 4.7%
  • Sheep milk: 4.3%
  • Camel milk: 5.6% (highest)
  • Sow milk: 3.4% (lowest)
Key Facts About Lactose
  • Lactose is the least variable component of milk.
  • It is present as a true solution in milk.
  • Known as milk sugar — responsible for the mild sweetness of milk.
  • Lactose and chloride together are primarily responsible for depressing the freezing point of milk.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 5.2% & 4.9% → values are reversed (cow/buffalo swapped).
  • 4.5% & 4.8% → not the correct values for either species.

posts.post_title: Milk Sugar
posts.post_content: Which is known as milk sugar?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lactose

Lactose is known as milk sugar. It is a disaccharide composed of glucose + galactose linked by a β-1,4-glycosidic bond. It is the principal carbohydrate in milk and is found almost exclusively in milk and dairy products.

Key Properties of Lactose
  • Present in milk as a true solution.
  • Least variable component of milk.
  • Average content: Cow milk 4.9%; Buffalo milk 5.2%; Camel milk 5.6% (highest).
  • Responsible for the mild sweetness of milk.
  • Along with chloride, it is primarily responsible for depressing the freezing point of milk below 0°C.
  • During fermentation (e.g., dahi making), bacteria convert lactose → lactic acid (souring of milk).
Lactose Intolerance

Lactose intolerance is caused by deficiency of lactase enzyme in the small intestine, preventing hydrolysis of lactose. Undigested lactose passes to the large intestine where it is fermented by bacteria → gas, bloating, diarrhoea.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Lactic acid → product of lactose fermentation; not a sugar.
  • Glucose & Galactose → monosaccharide components of lactose after hydrolysis; not called 'milk sugar' themselves.

4. Specific gravity of milkd. Zeiss apparatus
5. Surface tension of milke. Centipoise

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 1-e, 2-d, 3-b, 4-a, 5-c

The correct matching of milk physical properties with their instruments/units is:

  • 1. Viscosity → e. Centipoise (unit of viscosity; whole milk ~1.5–2.0 centipoise at 25°C)
  • 2. Refractive index → d. Zeiss apparatus (Zeiss Refractometer; value: 1.344–1.348 at 20°C)
