posts.post_title: Major Immunoglobulin in Ruminant Milk
posts.post_content: Major immunoglobulin present in human milk is IgA, but in ruminant milk the major immunoglobulin is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgG

The major immunoglobulin in ruminant milk (bovine colostrum) is IgG, whereas in human milk/colostrum, the major immunoglobulin is IgA.

Immunoglobulins in Bovine Colostrum (Decreasing Order)
  • IgG₁ > IgG₂ > IgM > IgA
  • All these are present: IgG1, IgG2, IgM, IgA
Why This Matters — Passive Immunity in Calves
  • In ruminants, placental transfer of antibodies does NOT occur (syndesmochorial placenta), so the newborn calf is born without circulating antibodies.
  • The calf must absorb immunoglobulins directly from colostrum through the gut wall (gut closure occurs within 24–36 hours after birth).
  • IgG from colostrum enters the bloodstream and provides systemic passive immunity.
Human vs. Ruminant — Key Differences
  • Human colostrum → IgA predominant (protects mucosal surfaces)
  • Bovine colostrum → IgG predominant (provides systemic immunity)

posts.post_title: Pulsation Ratio of Milking Machine for Cattle
posts.post_content: Pulsation ratio of milking machine in case of cattle is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 60/40

The pulsation ratio of a milking machine for cattle is 60/40 (i.e., 60% milking phase and 40% rest/massage phase per cycle).

Pulsation Ratio by Animal
  • Cattle: 60/40
  • Buffalo: 50/50 (equal milking and rest phases)
Other Milking Machine Parameters
  • Pulsation rate: 60 cycles/min (optimum)
  • Ideal vacuum — Cattle: 352 mmHg; Buffalo: 400 mmHg
  • Recommended vacuum: 10–15 inches of mercury
  • Minimum herd size: 20 animals
  • Pulsator = 'heart of milking machine'
Why the Ratio Differs
  • Buffalo teats have a narrower streak canal and tighter sphincter, requiring a balanced 50/50 ratio for effective milking.
  • Cattle teats allow a longer milking phase (60%) as milk let-down is more efficient.

posts.post_title: Index Organism for Pasteurization
posts.post_content: The index organism for pasteurization is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Coxiella burnetti

Coxiella burnetti is the index organism for pasteurization. It is the causative agent of Q-fever and is the most heat-resistant pathogen that is destroyed by pasteurization. If pasteurization conditions (72°C/15 sec for HTST) are adequate to destroy C. burnetti, all other milk-borne pathogens are also destroyed.

Key Features of Coxiella burnetti
  • Causes Q-fever (Query fever) in humans — an occupational hazard for farmers, abattoir workers, and veterinarians.
  • It is an obligate intracellular parasite (rickettsial organism).
  • It forms spore-like structures making it heat-resistant.
  • Transmitted via raw milk, aerosols, and contact with infected animal products.
Why the Phosphatase Test is Used

Phosphatase enzyme is naturally present in raw milk and is completely destroyed at pasteurization temperatures. So phosphatase test of pasteurized milk should be negative — a positive result means pasteurization was inadequate.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Mycobacterium tuberculosis → causes bovine TB (milk-borne disease), but is less heat-resistant than C. burnetti.
  • Leptospira → causes Leptospirosis; also milk-borne but less heat-resistant.
  • Listeria → causes Listeriosis; important food safety pathogen but not the index organism for pasteurization.

posts.post_title: Phospholipids in Milk
posts.post_content: Phospholipid(s) present in milk is/are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above — Lecithin, Cephalin, Sphingomyelin

Milk fat contains three major phospholipids: Lecithin, Cephalin (Phosphatidylethanolamine), and Sphingomyelin. These are present in the fat globule membrane that surrounds each fat droplet in milk.

Role of Phospholipids in Milk
  • Lecithin is the most important phospholipid — it acts as an excellent emulsifying agent that stabilizes the fat-in-water emulsion in milk. It has both hydrophilic (water-loving) and hydrophobic (fat-loving) ends, allowing it to bridge the fat-water interface.
  • Cephalin: Also present in the fat globule membrane; contributes to membrane integrity.
  • Sphingomyelin: Found in the outer layer of the fat globule membrane; has roles in cellular signaling.
Fat Components in Milk

Milk fat includes:

  • Triglycerides (major fraction, ~98%)
  • Phospholipids (Lecithin, Cephalin, Sphingomyelin)
  • Cholesterol
  • Carotene
  • Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)

posts.post_title: Properties of Milk Lactose
posts.post_content: Which is true about milk lactose?

_aimcq_options.text: Least variable component of milk only
Lactose is present in milk in the form of true solution only
Average lactose content of cow & buffalo milk is 4.5% & 4.8% respectively only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All the above

All three statements about milk lactose are correct:

  1. Least variable component of milk: Unlike fat (which varies enormously with breed, stage of lactation, time of milking), lactose content remains remarkably constant across conditions. This is because lactose synthesis in the mammary gland is tightly regulated — it is the primary osmotic regulator of milk volume.
  2. Present as true solution: Lactose molecules dissolve completely in the aqueous phase of milk at molecular level — they are not colloidal or emulsified.
  3. Average lactose content: Cow milk = 4.9% (≈ 4.5% is sometimes cited in older references but 4.9% is from composition table); Buffalo milk = 5.2% (≈ 4.8% older reference). The answer key accepts 4.5% & 4.8% as per the question's own options.
Why Lactose Controls Milk Volume

Lactose is the main osmotic agent in milk. Since milk is isotonic with blood plasma, the amount of lactose synthesized by the mammary gland determines how much water is drawn into milk. More lactose synthesis → more milk volume.

posts.post_title: Yield of Khoa from Cow and Buffalo Milk
posts.post_content: The yield of Khoa from cow milk and buffalo milk respectively is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 18%, 22%

The normal yield of Khoa is approximately 17–19% from cow milk (average ~18%) and 21–23% from buffalo milk (average ~22%).

Why Buffalo Milk Gives Higher Yield
  • Buffalo milk has much higher total solids (15.8%) compared to cow milk (13.4%).
  • Higher fat content in buffalo milk (6.6%) vs cow milk (4.6%) directly increases Khoa yield.
  • Hence, buffalo milk is always preferred for Khoa making.
Chemical Composition of Khoa
ComponentCow Milk KhoaBuffalo Milk Khoa
Moisture25.6%19.2%
Fat25.7%37.1%
Iron103 ppm101 ppm

posts.post_content: Pasteurization of milk under reduced pressure by direct steam is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vacuum pasteurization

Vacuum pasteurization (Vacreation) is the process of pasteurizing milk under reduced pressure using direct steam, carried out by a Vacreator instrument.

posts.post_title: Biological Value of Cow and Buffalo Milk
posts.post_content: The biological value of cow milk and buffalo milk respectively is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 86.90 and 84.04

The biological value (BV) of cow milk is 86.90 and of buffalo milk is 84.04.

What is Biological Value?

Biological Value (BV) measures the proportion of absorbed protein from food that becomes incorporated into body proteins. A higher BV means better protein quality for growth and maintenance.

Key Protein Facts
  • Cow milk proteins have high digestibility and high biological value compared to buffalo milk.
  • Milk proteins are rich in essential amino acids, particularly Lysine and Valine.
  • Cow milk is a better source of high-quality protein despite buffalo milk having more total protein (3.9% vs 3.4%).

posts.post_title: Primary Function of Colostrum Feeding in Calves
posts.post_content: The primary function of colostrum feeding in calves is:

_aimcq_options.text: Act as laxative and clear the meconium

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: To fortify calf's disease resistance

The primary function of colostrum feeding in calves is to fortify the calf's disease resistance by providing immunoglobulins (passive immunity). Since ruminant placenta (syndesmochorial type) does not allow transfer of maternal antibodies, the calf is born immunocompromised and entirely dependent on colostrum.

All Benefits of Colostrum Feeding
  • ✔ Provides passive immunity (IgG, IgM, IgA — primarily IgG)
  • ✔ Acts as a laxative to clear meconium (first faeces)
  • ✔ Rich in Vitamin A (5–15× normal milk)
  • ✔ Contains trypsin inhibitor protecting immunoglobulins from GIT digestion
  • ✔ Higher fat and total solids than normal milk
Important Protocol
  • Colostrum should be fed within 6–12 hours of birth (before gut closure begins).
  • Fed @ 10% of body weight daily for the first 3–4 days.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Act as laxative → this is a secondary benefit, not the primary function.
  • Accelerate weight gain → not the primary reason; energy content is not the key goal.
  • Thermoregulation → not a documented primary function of colostrum feeding.

posts.post_title: Ideal Vacuum of Milking Machine for Cattle
posts.post_content: Ideal vacuum of milking machine in case of cattle is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 352 mmHg

The ideal vacuum for milking machine in case of cattle is 352 mmHg. For buffalo, the ideal vacuum is 400 mmHg.

Milking Machine Vacuum Settings
  • Cattle: 352 mmHg
  • Buffalo: 400 mmHg (higher vacuum needed due to narrower teat canal)
  • General recommendation: 10–15 inches of mercury
Why Different Vacuums?
  • Buffaloes have a tighter teat sphincter and smaller teat orifice compared to cattle.
  • Higher vacuum (400 mmHg) is required to effectively open the teat canal and allow milk flow in buffaloes.
Complete Milking Machine Parameters Summary
  • Pulsation rate: 60 cycles/min
  • Pulsation ratio: Cattle 60/40; Buffalo 50/50
  • Ideal vacuum: Cattle 352 mmHg; Buffalo 400 mmHg
  • Minimum herd size: 20 animals

posts.post_title: By-product of Cheese Making
posts.post_content: By-product of cheese is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Whey

Whey is the liquid by-product obtained during cheese (and also Channa/Paneer) making. When milk is coagulated (by rennet or acid) and the curd is separated, the remaining greenish-yellow liquid is called whey.

Whey Characteristics
  • Contains whey proteins (α-lactalbumin & β-lactoglobulin), lactose, minerals.
  • Greenish-yellow colour is due to Riboflavin (Vitamin B2).
  • Rich in water-soluble vitamins and lactose.
By-products of Other Dairy Products
  • Cheese making: Whey ✔
  • Butter making: Buttermilk (Lassi/Chhaas) is the by-product
  • Cream separation: Skim milk is the by-product
  • Ghee making: Ghee residue (milk solids)
Bluish Colour of Skim Milk

Skim milk appears bluish because after fat removal, riboflavin's colour is more prominent and there is no carotene/fat to give yellowish tint.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Buttermilk → by-product of butter churning, not cheese.
  • Skim milk → by-product of cream separation, not cheese.
  • Butter oil → a clarified fat product, not a cheese by-product.

posts.post_title: Emulsifying Agent in Milk Fat
posts.post_content: An excellent emulsifying agent which stabilizes the milk fat emulsion is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lecithin

Lecithin (a phospholipid) is the excellent emulsifying agent in milk that stabilizes the fat-in-water emulsion. It is amphiphilic — having a polar (hydrophilic) phosphate-containing head and a non-polar (hydrophobic) fatty acid tail — allowing it to position at the oil-water interface and prevent fat globules from coalescing.

Why Lecithin is an Ideal Emulsifier
  • Its hydrophobic tail embeds in the fat globule.
  • Its hydrophilic head faces the aqueous phase.
  • This creates a stable protective membrane around each fat globule.
  • Result: Fat stays dispersed as tiny droplets (2–5 µm) in the aqueous phase → stable emulsion.
Industrial Application

Lecithin (often from soy or egg yolk) is widely used as an emulsifier in food industry — in chocolate, margarine, ice cream, baked goods, and salad dressings.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Lipid → lipids are the fat themselves, not an emulsifier.
  • Wax → a type of lipid with no emulsifying function in milk.
  • Lactose → a sugar in true solution; has no emulsifying properties.

posts.post_title: Casein Content of Buffalo and Cow Milk
posts.post_content: The Casein contents of buffalo milk & cow milk are respectively:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Buffalo 4.3% & Cow 3%

Buffalo milk contains 4.3% casein and Cow milk contains 3% casein. Buffalo milk has significantly more casein than cow milk, which is why buffalo milk is preferred for making khoa, paneer, and other casein-rich products.

Casein in Milk
  • Casein is present in milk as a colloidal suspension of calcium-caseinate-phosphate complex.
  • It constitutes approximately 80% of total milk protein.
  • Casein exists in three forms: α, β, γ casein.
  • α-casein has two components: αs-casein (calcium-sensitive) and K-casein (calcium-insensitive).
  • K-casein acts as a protective colloid, stabilizing casein micelles.
  • Rennet (chymosin) acts on K-casein → destabilizes micelles → milk coagulates (basis of cheese making).
Casein and White Colour

Casein's large colloidal micelles scatter all wavelengths of visible light equally → milk appears white. Buffalo milk is whiter than cow milk partly due to higher casein content.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 3% & 4.3% → values are reversed (buffalo and cow swapped).
  • 4% & 3% → 4% is close for buffalo but 4.3% is the correct value.
  • 5% & 7% → fabricated values; no standard reference supports these.

posts.post_title: Flavouring Agent in Butter
posts.post_content: The flavouring agent used in butter is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Diacetyl

Diacetyl is the principal flavouring agent used in butter, giving it its characteristic aroma. Its content in butter should not exceed 4 ppm.

Key Components of Butter
  • Flavouring agent: Diacetyl (≤4 ppm)
  • Colouring agent: Annatto (gives yellow colour to butter)
  • Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K — all present in butter
  • Butter is a Water-in-Fat type emulsion.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Annatto — colouring agent (yellow colour), not flavouring.
  • Cane sugar & Gelatin — thickening agents used in milk; not flavouring agents in butter.

posts.post_title: Significance of Coliform Bacteria in Milk
posts.post_content: The presence of coliform bacteria in milk is indicative of:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Faecal contamination

Coliform bacteria (mainly Escherichia coli) in milk are indicator organisms for faecal contamination. Their presence signifies that the milk has been contaminated with material of faecal origin, indicating poor hygiene during milking or processing.

Key Quality Tests and Their Significance
  • Coliform count test → Faecal contamination ✔
  • Phosphatase test → Inadequacy of pasteurization
  • Methylene blue / Resazurin test → Bacterial contamination (extent)
  • Hansa test → Mixing of cow & buffalo milk
  • Organoleptic test → Colour, flavour, taste
Index Organism for Pasteurization

Coxiella burnetti (Q-fever agent) — most heat-resistant pathogen destroyed by pasteurization.

posts.post_title: Essential Amino Acids in Which Milk Proteins Are Rich
posts.post_content: Milk proteins contain essential amino acids in adequate amounts. They are particularly rich in:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lysine and Valine

Milk proteins are particularly rich in the essential amino acids Lysine and Valine.

Nutritional Significance
  • Lysine — a limiting amino acid in many cereal-based diets; milk is an excellent complementary protein source.
  • Valine — a branched-chain amino acid (BCAA) important for muscle metabolism and tissue repair.
Milk Protein Classification
  • Casein (80%): α, β, γ-casein — forms calcium-caseinate-phosphate complex
  • Whey proteins (20%): α-Lactalbumin, β-Lactoglobulin
Biological Value of Milk Proteins
  • Cow milk BV: 86.90 | Buffalo milk BV: 84.04
  • Cow milk proteins have high digestibility and high BV

posts.post_title: Immunoglobulins Present in Bovine Milk
posts.post_content: Immunoglobulins present in bovine milk are:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: IgG1, IgG2, IgM and IgA

All four immunoglobulins — IgG1, IgG2, IgM, and IgA — are present in bovine milk (and colostrum). However, their concentration differs significantly.

Order of Immunoglobulins in Bovine Colostrum (Decreasing Concentration)
  • IgG₁ > IgG₂ > IgM > IgA
Immune Factors in Bovine Colostrum
  • Lactoferrin (iron-binding protein, important during mammary involution)
  • Immunoglobulins (IgG1, IgG2, IgM, IgA)
  • Trypsin inhibitor (protects immunoglobulins from GIT digestion in newborn calf)
Comparison
  • Major Ig in bovine colostrum: IgG
  • Major Ig in human colostrum: IgA

posts.post_title: Official Test for Milk Sterilization Efficiency
posts.post_content: The official test for judging the efficiency of sterilization of milk is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Turbidity test

The official test for judging the efficiency of sterilization of milk is the Turbidity test.

Important Distinction — Sterilization vs. Pasteurization Tests
  • Turbidity test: Used to detect adequacy of sterilization (the official test for sterilized milk).
  • Phosphatase test: Used to detect inadequacy of pasteurization (NOT applicable to sterilized milk — phosphatase is already destroyed at pasteurization temperatures; sterilization goes far beyond that).
Why Phosphatase Test is Not Used for Sterilization
  • Phosphatase enzyme is destroyed at pasteurization temperature (72°C/15 sec).
  • Sterilization uses much higher temperatures (110–121°C), so phosphatase would already be absent — the test would be positive (no phosphatase) but cannot distinguish between pasteurized and sterilized milk.
  • The Turbidity test uses the heat-coagulable whey proteins to distinguish sterilization from pasteurization.
Other Quality Tests for Reference
  • COB test: Heat stability of milk
  • Dye reduction test: Extent of bacterial contamination
  • Coliform count: Faecal contamination

posts.post_title: Peak Milk Yield in Dairy Cattle
posts.post_content: Peak milk yield in dairy cattle occurs at:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 6–8 weeks of lactation

Peak milk yield in dairy cattle occurs at 6–8 weeks (approximately 40–60 days) after parturition. Milk production rises steeply after calving, reaches its peak at 6–8 weeks, and then gradually declines over the rest of the lactation period.

Lactation Phases in Dairy Cattle
  • Early phase (1–100 days): Milk yield increases rapidly; peaks at 6–8 weeks.
  • Mid-phase (101–200 days): Dry matter intake peaks; milk yield begins declining.
  • Late phase (201–305 days): Milk yield declines steadily toward dry-off.
Lactation in Which Maximum Lifetime Yield Occurs
  • Cow: Maximum milk yield in 4th–6th lactation.
  • Buffalo: Maximum milk yield in 4th lactation.
Standard Lactation Period

Standard lactation period = 305 days (10 months). Calving interval = 365 days (12 months) = Lactation (305 days) + Dry period (60 days).

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 4–6 weeks → too early; peak has not been reached yet.
  • 8–12 weeks → too late; production is usually declining by this point.
  • 2–4 weeks → this is immediately post-calving; milk production is still ramping up.

posts.post_title: Blood Required per ml of Milk Produced
posts.post_content: For the production of 1 ml of milk, the quantity of blood that passes through secretory tissues of the mammary gland is about:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 500 ml

Approximately 400–500 ml of blood must pass through the secretory tissues of the mammary gland to produce 1 ml of milk. This enormous blood flow is necessary because milk synthesis requires continuous delivery of precursors (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, minerals, vitamins) from blood to mammary secretory cells (alveolar epithelial cells).

Circulatory System of the Udder
  • Arterial supply: External pudic artery (mammary artery)
  • Venous return (3 primary routes):
    1. Subcutaneous abdominal vein (milk vein) — 1st route; acts as an index of milking ability (prominent milk vein = high yielder)
    2. External pudic vein — 2nd route
    3. Perineal vein — 3rd route
Practical Significance

The blood-to-milk ratio (500:1) explains why high-producing cows have visibly prominent milk veins and why mammary health is so critical — any disruption in blood flow (e.g., mastitis-related inflammation, injury) directly reduces milk synthesis.

Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • 100 ml → far too low; not enough to supply all milk precursors.
  • 1000 ml → overestimate; 500 ml is the accepted figure.
  • 200 ml → insufficient; documented requirement is 400–500 ml.

posts.post_title: Detection of Vanaspati Adulteration in Milk Fat
posts.post_content: Adulteration of milk fat with hydrogenated vegetable oils like vanaspati is detected by:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Baudoin test

The Baudoin test (also spelled Baudouin test) is used to detect adulteration of milk fat (ghee, butter) with hydrogenated vegetable oils (vanaspati/dalda). The test detects sesame oil (til oil), which is mandatorily added to vanaspati in India as a marker.

Principle of Baudoin Test

Vanaspati is required by law to contain at least 5% sesame oil as a marker. The Baudoin test uses furfural reagent — sesame oil contains sesamol/sesamin that gives a red colour with furfural + hydrochloric acid. A positive Baudoin test (red colour) indicates presence of vanaspati in milk fat.

Other Detection Tests
  • Hansa test: Mixing of cow & buffalo milk
  • Iodine test: Starch adulteration in milk
  • Benedict test: Reducing sugars (not milk adulteration)
  • Bromo-cresol-purple: Detergent adulteration
  • p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde: Urea adulteration
  • Picric acid: Gelatin adulteration
  • Delvo kit: Antibiotic residues
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Benedict test → detects reducing sugars; not used for fat adulteration.
  • Hansa test → detects species mixing (cow vs. buffalo), not vanaspati.
  • Iodine test → detects starch, not vanaspati.

posts.post_title: Diacetyl Content in Butter
posts.post_content: The Diacetyl content in butter should not exceed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 4 ppm

The flavouring agent Diacetyl in butter must not exceed 4 ppm (parts per million) as per standards.

Role of Diacetyl in Butter
  • Diacetyl is a volatile diketone compound responsible for the characteristic buttery flavour and aroma.
  • It is produced during fermentation of cream (by Streptococcus lactis subsp. diacetylactis and Leuconostoc species).
  • Excess Diacetyl can cause off-flavours and is therefore regulated.
Other Key Butter Facts
  • Butter = Water-in-Fat emulsion
  • Colouring agent: Annatto
  • Fishy odour in butter = due to rancidity
  • Contains all fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K

posts.post_title: Test to Detect Inadequacy of Pasteurization
posts.post_content: The test used to detect inadequacy of pasteurization is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Phosphatase test

The Phosphatase test is used to detect inadequacy of pasteurization. Phosphatase enzyme is naturally present in raw milk and is completely destroyed during pasteurization. If phosphatase activity is detected in supposedly pasteurized milk, it indicates that pasteurization was incomplete or inadequate.

Key Distinction
  • Phosphatase test → Inadequacy of pasteurization ✔
  • Turbidity test → Official test for judging efficiency of sterilization (not applicable to pasteurization)
  • Catalase test → Detection of mastitis or abnormal milk
  • Resazurin test → Dye reduction test to assess bacterial contamination
Why Phosphatase?

Phosphatase has almost the same heat resistance as Mycobacterium tuberculosis, making it a reliable indicator — if phosphatase is destroyed, dangerous pathogens are also destroyed.

posts.post_title: Factor Determining Colour of Milk Fat
posts.post_content: The colour of milk fat is dependent upon its:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Carotene content

The colour of milk fat is determined by its β-Carotene (Carotene) content.

Carotene and Milk Colour
  • Cow milk: Yellow/creamy colour — cows cannot fully convert β-carotene to Vitamin A, so excess carotene gives fat its yellow tint.
  • Buffalo milk: White — buffaloes efficiently convert all β-carotene to Vitamin A; no residual carotene remains to colour the fat.
  • Grass-fed cattle: More yellow milk (higher carotene from green fodder)
  • Stall-fed cattle: White-yellowish milk (lower carotene)
Other Milk Colour Facts
  • Greenish-yellow colour of whey → Riboflavin
  • Bluish colour of skim milk → Riboflavin
  • White colour of buffalo milk → Casein protein

posts.post_title: Organ Producing Pigeon Milk
posts.post_content: 'Pigeon Milk' is a white slimy substance produced by the:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Crop

'Pigeon milk' is a white slimy substance produced by the crop of pigeons (specifically crop-lining cells of both male and female pigeons). It is NOT produced by a mammary gland — birds do not have mammary glands.

What is Pigeon Milk?
  • It is a crop secretion (not true milk) rich in protein and fat.
  • Produced under the influence of the hormone prolactin (same hormone that stimulates mammary milk production in mammals).
  • Both parent pigeons (male and female) produce it to feed squabs (baby pigeons) during the first few days after hatching.
  • It is analogous to mammalian milk in function but differs in origin.
Mammary Gland Facts
  • Mammary glands are modified sudoriferous (sweat) glands — ectodermal in origin.
  • Mammary glands are innervated only with sympathetic fibres; parasympathetic fibres are absent in udder.
Why Other Options Are Wrong
  • Mammary gland → birds do not have mammary glands.
  • Gizzard → a muscular digestive organ; not involved in milk-like secretion.
  • Both crop and mammary gland → incorrect; only the crop is involved.

posts.post_title: Forequarters to Hindquarters Milk Ratio in Cattle
posts.post_content: The ratio of forequarters milk to hindquarters milk in cattle is:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 40:60

In cattle, the ratio of forequarters milk : hindquarters milk is 40:60. The hindquarters produce more milk (60%) than the forequarters (40%) due to their larger glandular tissue volume.

Practical Significance
  • In cases of quarter-specific mastitis, the affected quarter's contribution can be assessed by separate quarter milking.
  • The greater yield of hindquarters is considered in teat cup cluster design for milking machines.
Related Udder Facts
  • There is no communication among all 4 quarters of the udder — minimizes spread of infection.
  • 400–500 ml blood passes through the udder to produce 1 ml of milk.
  • Subcutaneous abdominal vein (milk vein) acts as an index for milking ability.
